title: Knowledge check: Contributing to Existing R Packages

questions.prompt: For “Contributing to Existing R Packages”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: A maintainable R package needs clear metadata, namespaces, dependencies, documentation, tests and checks before release. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Contributing to Existing R Packages” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Reading an Unfamiliar Codebase” as part of lesson 219. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Contributing to Existing R Packages” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Identify the package files involved and name one test or check that should pass before publishing. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
